4076784.note: Alabama's capital since 1846, it was the first capital of the Confederacy — and a century later, the endpoint of the Selma to Montgomery marches. Rosa Parks' 1955 bus boycott began on its streets.

4119403.note: Central High School here was the 1957 desegregation battleground, where the Little Rock Nine braved mobs under federal guard.

4137672.note: When the Civil War ended, freed families told General Howard exactly what they needed: "Land! Give us land!" In 1867 the Freedmen's Bureau bought this 375-acre farm in southeast Washington, D.C. and sold it in one-acre pieces families could afford — it grew into Barry Farm, a proud, self-built Black community. 🎉 Fun twist: it's named for James Barry, the merchant and councilman who owned this farm — not Mayor Marion Barry (he chose the name "Barry" himself back in college). Same spelling, total coincidence!

4142290.note: Delaware was the first state to ratify the Constitution — hence 'the First State.' Dover has been its capital since 1777.

4174715.note: Chosen as capital in 1824 as the midpoint between St. Augustine and Pensacola. Its name is Muskogean for 'old town.'

4180439.note: Burned by Sherman in 1864, it rose to host the 1996 Olympics. Martin Luther King Jr. was born here.

4250542.note: Lincoln lived here 24 years before the presidency, and his tomb still draws pilgrims from around the world.

4259418.note: The Indy 500 has run at the Brickyard since 1911. The Soldiers and Sailors Monument anchors the city's center.

4280539.note: Brown v. Board of Education began here — the 1954 ruling that ended school segregation nationwide.

4292188.note: Named for pioneer Stephen Frank, killed at the river ford in 1780. Daniel Boone is buried in its cemetery.

4315588.note: French for 'red stick,' a boundary marker seen by explorers in 1699. Its 34-story Capitol is the tallest state capitol in America.

4347242.note: The U.S. Naval Academy has trained officers here since 1845. Congress ratified the Treaty of Paris in its State House.

4392388.note: Named for Thomas Jefferson while he was still alive. Its 1836–2004 state penitentiary was the oldest operating prison west of the Mississippi — 'the bloodiest 47 acres in America.'

4431410.note: Named for Andrew Jackson and burned three times in the Civil War — Sherman's men called it 'Chimneyville.'

4487042.note: Named for Sir Walter Raleigh, sponsor of the Lost Colony. It anchors the Research Triangle.

4509177.note: Named for Christopher Columbus and now America's 14th-largest city. Ohio State's campus fuels its growth.

4544349.note: Born in a single day — the 1889 Land Run staked thousands of claims by sunset. Its memorial honors the 1995 bombing victims.

4575352.note: Sherman's troops burned it in 1865 — who started the fire is still debated. The University of South Carolina was founded here in 1801.

4644585.note: Music City — the Grand Ole Opry has broadcast here since 1925. Its full-scale Parthenon replica earned it 'Athens of the South.'

4671654.note: Named for Stephen F. Austin, 'Father of Texas.' 'Keep Austin Weird' and its live-music scene define it.

4781708.note: Capital of the Confederacy; its fall in 1865 ended the Civil War. Patrick Henry's 'Give me liberty' speech rang out here.

4801859.note: Named for early settler Charles Clendenin. Its gold-leaf Capitol dome gleams over the Kanawha River.

4835797.note: Mark Twain wrote his most famous books in his Hartford home, now a museum. Insurance wealth once made it one of America's richest cities.

4853828.note: Its name is French for 'of the monks.' Every four years the Iowa caucuses put it at the center of presidential politics.

4930956.note: The Freedom Trail walks the Revolution: the Tea Party, Paul Revere's ride, Bunker Hill. Harvard, founded 1636, is across the river.

4957003.note: Named for the daughter of Revolutionary War general Henry Dearborn. It is one of America's smallest capitals.

4998830.note: Made capital in 1847 to move government inland from border-town Detroit. It is named for Lansing, New York, an early settler's hometown.

5045360.note: The head of Mississippi River navigation made it a fur-trade hub. F. Scott Fitzgerald was born here.

5072006.note: Renamed for Abraham Lincoln after his assassination — the first city to bear his name. Its 400-foot Capitol tower is a landmark for miles.

5084868.note: Named for harmony after a boundary dispute was settled. Christa McAuliffe taught here before the Challenger mission.

5105496.note: Washington's Christmas-night crossing and the 1776 Battle of Trenton turned the Revolution's tide.

5106834.note: Chartered in 1686, among America's oldest cities. The Erie Canal made it a 19th-century boomtown.

5192726.note: A key Underground Railroad crossing on the Susquehanna. Three Mile Island's 1979 accident happened just downstream.

5224151.note: Founded 1636 by Roger Williams as a haven for religious freedom. Brown University has stood on College Hill since 1764.

5238685.note: America's smallest capital, under 8,000 people. Named for Montpellier, France.

5261457.note: Built on an isthmus between two lakes and named for James Madison. Its Capitol dome is the largest granite dome in the world.

5308655.note: America's hottest major city, built over ancient Hohokam canals. It is now the fifth-largest city in the United States.

5389489.note: Born in the Gold Rush and capital since 1854. The western end of the Transcontinental Railroad was built here.

5419384.note: The Mile High City — a medallion on the Capitol steps marks exactly 5,280 feet. It boomed on Pikes Peak gold.

5490263.note: America's oldest capital city, founded in 1610 — a decade before the Pilgrims landed. Its adobe Plaza still anchors downtown.

5501344.note: Named for Kit Carson and built on Comstock Lode silver. Its U.S. Mint stamped the coveted 'CC' coins.

5554072.note: Alaska's capital is unreachable by road — you can only arrive by boat or plane. It was named for Joe Juneau, a gold prospector who struck it rich here in 1880.

5586437.note: French-Canadian trappers named it crying 'les bois!' — 'the woods!' It is pronounced BOY-see, never boy-ZEE.

5656882.note: Born as 'Last Chance Gulch' in the 1864 gold rush. Its grand Capitol rose on copper-boom money.

5688025.note: Named for Germany's Otto von Bismarck to lure railroad investment. Its 19-story Capitol is the 'Skyscraper on the Prairie.'

5750162.note: Named for the Hebrew word for peace. It grew rich on Willamette Valley hops and cherries.

5767918.note: One of America's smallest capitals, on the Missouri River. It took the title at statehood in 1889.

5780993.note: Founded 1847 by Brigham Young and Mormon pioneers. Temple Square anchors its downtown.

5805687.note: Named for the Olympic Mountains across Puget Sound. Its downtown artesian well still flows with free spring water.

5821086.note: Named for the Cheyenne Nation and raised on railroad money. Frontier Days, running since 1897, is billed as the world's largest rodeo.

5856195.note: The only U.S. state capital with a royal palace — ʻIolani Palace housed Hawaii's last monarchs. Pearl Harbor lies just west.

_comment: Curated memorable facts for notable GeoNames places, keyed by geonameid. Merged into blurbs at dataset build time (scripts/build-geonames-dataset.mjs). Every note is a verifiable fact in the starters' voice: 1-2 sentences, evocative, no filler. wiki is the en.wikipedia.org article slug for attribution.

1269843.note: Founded in 1591 beyond the fortified Golconda; its Charminar has come to symbolize the city. Since the 1990s it has emerged as an Indian IT hub around HITEC City, and Guinness World Records declared its Ramoji Film City the world's largest film studio.

104515.note: Considered the birthplace of Islam and the holiest city in the faith, it is home to the Kaaba, the direction of prayer for Muslims worldwide. Pilgrims more than triple its population each year during the Ḥajj, the pilgrimage every Muslim must make at least once in life.

170654.note: The oldest capital city in the world, first settled in the 3rd millennium BC, it served as capital of the Umayyad Caliphate from 661 to 750. Its ancient city is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the English word 'damask' comes from its Silk Road silks.

2542997.note: Founded around 1070 as the Almoravid capital, it is one of Morocco's four imperial cities — and the whole country was long known abroad as the Kingdom of Marrakesh. Its red-walled medina, the 'Red City', is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

264371.note: One of the world's oldest cities, with recorded history spanning over 3,400 years; classical Athens was a centre of ancient Greek democracy and is often regarded as its birthplace. Its Parthenon crowns the Acropolis, and it hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896.

2643743.note: Founded by the Romans as Londinium around AD 47, it was the world's largest city from about 1831 to 1925. It runs the world's oldest rapid transit system, the London Underground, and is the first city to host three Summer Olympic Games.

2761369.note: A Roman camp called Vindobona in the 1st century, it became the seat of the Habsburg emperors of the Holy Roman Empire until 1806 and hosted the Congress of Vienna in 1814–15. It remains renowned as the home of Mozart, Beethoven, and the Viennese classical tradition.

281184.note: One of the world's oldest cities, with a history spanning over 5,000 years, it is considered a holy city to Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Its Old City holds the Western Wall, the Dome of the Rock, and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site in Danger.

2988507.note: First settled as the Roman town of Lutetia, it became the Frankish capital under Clovis in 508 and the centre stage of the French Revolution in 1789. Nicknamed the City of Light for its leading role in the Age of Enlightenment, it holds the Louvre, the world's largest and most-visited museum.

3067696.note: Capital of the Kingdom of Bohemia and residence of Holy Roman Emperors, it flourished under Charles IV, who founded Charles University — the oldest in Central Europe — in 1347. Its historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its 1410 astronomical clock still works.

3128760.note: Capital of the County of Barcelona and later the most important city of the Crown of Aragon, it hosted the 1992 Summer Olympics. The works of Antoni Gaudí are UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and its Taula de canvi, founded in 1401, is often viewed as Europe's oldest public bank.

3164603.note: Capital of the Republic of Venice for almost a millennium (810–1797), it grew from lagoon islands into a maritime power and the first real international financial centre. Built on 126 islands linked by 472 bridges, its lagoon is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

3169070.note: Its history spans 28 centuries, rising from a mythic 753 BC founding to capital of the Roman Kingdom, Republic, and Empire — the Eternal City and a cradle of Western civilization. Vatican City, the world's smallest country, sits entirely within its municipal boundaries.

3176959.note: Founded as a Roman garrison in 59 BC, it is considered the birthplace of the Renaissance and rose under the rule of the Medici family. The Florentine dialect forms the base of standard Italian, and its historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

360630.note: Founded in 969 as the Fatimid capital, it is the 'city of a thousand minarets'; the Giza pyramids and ancient Memphis lie within its bounds. Its historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and Al-Azhar is one of the world's oldest universities.

361058.note: Founded in 331 BC by Alexander the Great, it became the Ptolemaic capital and a leading hub of ancient science and scholarship. Its Great Library was the largest in the ancient world, and its Pharos lighthouse was one of the Seven Wonders.

745044.note: Founded as Byzantium by Greek colonists in the 7th century BC and reborn as Constantinople in 330 AD, it served as capital of four empires — Roman, Byzantine, Latin, and Ottoman — until 1922. Straddling two continents, its historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

98182.note: Founded in 762 AD by Caliph al-Mansur as the Abbasid capital, it became the 'Center of Learning' of the Islamic Golden Age, housing the House of Wisdom and rivalling Chang'an as the world's largest city. The Mongols largely destroyed it in 1258.

1816670.note: With over three millennia of recorded history, it has been China's political center for most of the past eight centuries. The Ming-era Forbidden City (built 1406-1420) anchors its eight UNESCO World Heritage Sites, and in 2022 it became the first city to host both the Summer and Winter Olympics.

1857910.note: Japan's imperial capital for over a thousand years, from 794 until the court moved to Tokyo in 1869. Spared from WWII bombing, its temples and shrines survive intact - 17 of them inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 1994.

1273294.note: Seat of the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire from the 13th to the 19th century, it is a city of seven historic cities. Its Qutub Minar, Humayun's Tomb, and Red Fort are UNESCO World Heritage Sites; New Delhi became the capital of British India in 1911.

1253405.note: One of the world's oldest continually inhabited cities, central to Hindu pilgrimage, death, and mourning on the Ganges. The Buddha gave his first sermon at nearby Sarnath in the fifth century BCE, and Adi Shankara established Shiva worship here in the 8th century.

1216265.note: A Silk Road crossroads among Central Asia's oldest continuously inhabited cities, conquered by Alexander the Great in 329 BC. Timur made it his imperial capital in the 14th century; its Registan Square anchors the UNESCO-listed 'Samarkand - Crossroads of Cultures'.

1609350.note: Founded as the capital by Rama I in 1782, after Thonburi (1767); it drove Siam's modernization in the late 19th century. Its full ceremonial name is the world's longest place name, and it has been named the world's most visited city.

1835848.note: Founded in 18 BC by the Baekje kingdom, it became the Joseon dynasty's planned capital in 1394. Devastated in the Korean War after changing hands four times, it rebuilt to host the 1988 Summer Olympics and became the national hub of the K-pop Korean Wave.

1822214.note: The gateway town to Angkor, the Khmer Empire's temple capital - Angkor Wat and Angkor Thom anchor the UNESCO World Heritage Site. Little more than a village when French explorers re-discovered Angkor in the 19th century, it is now Cambodia's second-largest city.

3530597.note: The oldest capital city in the Americas, founded as Tenochtitlan by the Mexica around 1325 on islands in Lake Texcoco. Razed after the 1521 siege and rebuilt to Spanish plans; today it is North America's most populous city.

3941584.note: Capital of the Inca Empire from the 13th century until the 1532 Spanish conquest, and Peru's constitutionally designated Historical Capital. Its Spanish colonial city rises over Inca stonework, and it is the gateway to Machu Picchu; UNESCO listed the 'City of Cusco' in 1983.

3652462.note: The oldest capital in South America, an Inca northern capital refounded by the Spanish in 1534. In 1978 it became one of the first sites ever inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List; at 2,850 m it is the capital closest to the Equator.

3687238.note: Founded in 1533, one of South America's oldest colonial cities; its port shipped Bolivian silver to Spain and received enslaved Africans under the asiento system. Its walled city and fortresses - built against Caribbean pirates - were listed by UNESCO in 1984.

5128581.note: The Dutch called it New Amsterdam until England seized it in 1664 and renamed it for the Duke of York. It was the young nation's first capital (1785–1790) — and in 1886 France gifted it the Statue of Liberty, which welcomed 14 million immigrants arriving through Ellis Island.

4887398.note: 'Chicago' comes from a Native word for wild onions. The Great Fire of 1871 left 100,000 homeless — but the city rebuilt with the world's first skyscraper (1885) and pulled off a legendary trick: in 1900 it made its river flow BACKWARD, away from Lake Michigan.

5368361.note: Founded in 1781 by 44 Spanish settlers as 'The Town of Our Lady the Queen of the Angels.' Hollywood merged in during 1910 — and by 1921, more than 80% of the world's movie-making happened here, making it the world capital of film.

5391959.note: Founded as a Spanish mission in 1776 and called Yerba Buena until 1847. The 1849 Gold Rush turned it into the West Coast's biggest city — then the 1906 earthquake and fire destroyed three-quarters of it, and the city rebuilt almost overnight. Its Golden Gate Bridge and cable cars are icons today.

4335045.note: Founded by the French in 1718 and named for the Duke of Orléans; it joined the U.S. in the 1803 Louisiana Purchase. Enslaved people were allowed to gather at Congo Square to play their native music — and from that, New Orleans gave birth to jazz in the early 1900s.

4164138.note: The only major U.S. city founded by a woman — citrus grower Julia Tuttle, 'the mother of Miami,' who talked a railroad tycoon into bringing his train here in 1896. It grew so fast winter visitors said it was like magic — hence 'Magic City.'

1275339.note: Built on seven islands that England got as part of a royal wedding dowry in 1661 (Catherine of Braganza's). Today it's India's financial capital — and the home of Bollywood, one of the world's biggest film industries.

1269515.note: One of modern India's earliest planned cities, founded in 1727 by king Jai Singh II. Painted pink in 1876 to welcome the Prince of Wales — it's been the 'Pink City' ever since, and today it's Rajasthan's capital.

1279259.note: The Mughal Empire's capital under five emperors, from Babur to Shah Jahan. Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal here (1632–1648) in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal — today the Taj and Agra Fort are both UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

2650225.note: Scotland's capital since at least the 1400s, crowned by a castle on an ancient volcanic rock. It's called the 'Athens of the North' — and its Fringe is the world's largest arts festival.

2643123.note: The world's first industrialised city — its cotton mills earned it the nickname 'Cottonopolis.' It also sat at one end of the world's first inter-city passenger railway, the Liverpool–Manchester line of 1830.

2640729.note: 'Oxford' means 'ford of the oxen' — a river crossing for cattle. It's home to the University of Oxford, the oldest university in the English-speaking world, teaching since the 11th century — and a 1209 town-vs-scholars feud sent fleeing academics off to found Cambridge.

4915989.note: This South Side Chicago neighborhood started as a railroad crossing called Junction Grove, settled by German and Swedish farmers in the 1840s. After the Great Chicago Fire of 1871, families fleeing the burned city rebuilt their lives here — and in 1889, Chicago annexed the whole town.
